front: TC004: What is the minimum viable move?
back: Name the fact that the last conversation was difficult — without over-explaining it — and say you want to move forward.

front: TC004: What is the core sequence?
back: Name the rupture lightly -> Take your part -> Reopen the door.

front: TC004: What is the field tip?
back: Repair the way it was said before what was said.

front: TC004: What is the strong version of: Pretending the rupture did not happen?
back: Last time was harder than I wanted. Can we come back to it?

front: TC004: What is the strong version of: Over-apologising to smooth it over without real repair?
back: Name what you did, own it specifically, then ask to move forward.

front: TC004: What is the strong version of: Bringing it up and immediately defending yourself?
back: I know I came in wrong there. I wanted to say that before we moved on.

front: TC004: What is better than: (Days of polite, careful silence)?
back: 'I did not want to leave it where it ended.'

front: TC004: What is better than: 'I am sorry you took it that way.'?
back: 'I am sorry for how I said it — it came out sharper than I meant.'

front: TC004: What is better than: 'You are right, it was all my fault, I am a nightmare.'?
back: 'My part was interrupting you. I can own that piece properly.'

front: TC004: What are signs it is working?
back: The other person softens or opens up after you name it. The air clears faster than you expected. You feel relieved rather than more exposed. Work or the relationship gets easier after the repair.

front: TC004: When should you avoid this technique?
back: When the other person needs space and is not ready to engage — forcing a repair can inflame. When you have no genuine ownership to take — empty apologies make ruptures worse.

front: TC004: What is the best recovery line?
back: 'I did not mean to reopen the argument — I wanted to close it.'
